articles.title: ‘Os sentidos do trabalho: Ensaio sobre a afirmação e a negação do trabalho’ by Ricardo Antunes
articles.author: Editor
articles.content: In 1999, the first edition of the Brazilian sociologist Ricardo Antunes’s The Meanings of Work [Os sentidos do trabalho] was published. Its stakes were clear: against the idea that new communication and automation technologies were announcing the “end of work”, Antunes insisted that work remained vital, both for capital and for humanity. The post ‘Os sentidos do trabalho: Ensaio sobre a afirmação e a negação do trabalho’ by Ricardo Antunes appeared first on MR Online .

articles.title: ICE is hiding detainees from their families – and the death toll is rising
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: ICE just scrubbed tens of thousands of people from its Online Detainee Locator System, leaving their families and legal teams in the dark. Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, joins Zoe Alexandra and Rania Khalek to break down how DHS effectively “disappeared” at least 20,000 people with final deportation orders, as deaths in custody climb and private prison giants GEO Group and CoreCivic rake in profits from ICE’s ballooning budget. Reichlin-Melnick explains how Trump’s mass deportation machine changed tactics after Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis and the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti – shifting to predawn raids, targeting people at airports and their own immigration check-ins, and quietly pushing arrests to 50,000 a month. Meanwhile, at least 60 people have died in ICE custody in Trump’s second term. Reichlin-Melnick says the real number is likely higher: ICE has stopped reporting deaths right after release, and cut inspections as it opens new facilities. Immigration is “a creature of Congress,” Reichlin-Melnick says, and what Congress gave ICE, it can take away. But with Trump’s veto looming, oversight may be lawmakers’ most powerful weapon. Will the new Democratic Congress rein it in? Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! #breakthroughnews

articles.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 | Propaganda for US war in Korea?
articles.author: Amanda Yee
articles.content: The new Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 just dropped, and it’s already mired in controversy. The game simulates urban warfare in Seoul, casting players as a South Korean marine fighting off an invasion from the DPRK. Is this video game harmless entertainment, or is it sophisticated imperialist propaganda designed to “manufacture consent” for war against North Korea and normalize US militarism? Ju-Hyun Park, organizer with Nodutdol for Korean Community Development and director of engagement at Breakthrough News, joins Amanda Yee to break down the dangerous political messaging behind Modern Warfare 4.

articles.title: Congolese president signs referendum bill that could allow for a third-term
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi has promulgated a controversial law establishing the conditions for holding referendums. Opposition parties, civil society groups and grassroots movements have previously said it could allow him to seek a third term. The signing follows more than five months of protests, court challenges, and street mobilization against the law. The promulgation was announced on national television late on Tuesday, November 10. “The President of the Republic, Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo, promulgated, on November 10, 2026, through an ordinance, the law setting the conditions for the organization of the referendum in the Democratic Republic of Congo,” state broadcaster RTNC reported. Roger Kalenga, Deputy Spokesperson for the Head of State, read excerpts of the new legislation on air: “Law No. 26/045 of November 9, 2026, establishing the conditions for organizing referendums in the DRC. … The National Assembly and the Senate have adopted, and the President of the Republic promulgates, the following law: Chapter One, Purpose and Scope. Article One: This law establishes the rules relating to the purpose, procedure, initiation, and convening of referendums, as well as related offenses.” The bill went through parliament, where Tshisekedi’s coalition holds a large majority, first passed it in June while opposition members stayed away. The Senate vote was 89 in favor, none against, with 20 senators not taking part. In July the Constitutional Court ruled the law constitutional, subject to interpretive reservations on thirteen provisions. On August 10, Tshisekedi sent the text back to parliament for a new deliberation, which re-adopted it in October. Read more: Push for referendum in DR Congo sparks protests over possible Tshisekedi third term The opposition opposes the referendum The law has met resistance at every stage. In May, the main opposition parties, formed Coalition Article 64 (C64) named after Article 64 of the constitution, which obliges every Congolese to oppose anyone who seizes power by force or exercises it in violation of the constitution. In mid-June, days before the Senate vote, opposition parties and civil society groups marched in Kinshasa against the bill. Police and security forces dispersed protesters with tear gas. Several people were injured. With opposition figures accusing the authorities of suppressing peaceful protest and violating citizens’ constitutional rights. Read more: Several arrested in protests against constitutional changes in DRC Protests rocked the country again on September 15, when C64 called a nationwide day of action. In Kinshasa, hundreds gathered before the march was disrupted by clashes with members of the Force du Progrès, a group affiliated with Tshisekedi’s UDPS party. Police fired tear gas and warning shots, and at least 10 people were arrested in Kinshasa. Constitutional limits and Tshisekedi’s third-term ambitions Tshisekedi, who first assumed office in January 2019 following the December 2018 elections, was re-elected in December 2023 for a second five-year term. Under the current constitution, his mandate is due to end in 2028. The current constitution limits the president to two five-year terms; However, the proposed constitutional changes have raised questions about whether a new constitution could be used to circumvent these protections. Tshisekedi has previously defended the possibility of constitutional reform and indicated his willingness to remain in office beyond 2028. In May 2026, he said he had not sought a third term but would accept one if the Congolese people wanted him to continue governing. The new referendum law therefore represents an important development in the dispute. Although it does not automatically remove presidential term limits or guarantee a third-term bid, it provides a legal framework for holding referendums on constitutional matters, including the adoption of a new Constitution. With the legislation now in force, opposition parties and civil society organisations face a renewed challenge in their campaign to defend the existing constitutional order.

articles.title: Keytruda was built on public science. Why does Merck own the rewards?
articles.author: David Franco
articles.content: Keytruda is often presented as the ultimate success story of modern pharmaceutical innovation. And in one sense, that is true. Few medicines have transformed oncology as profoundly as pembrolizumab. It has extended survival in melanoma, lung cancer, and many other malignancies, and it has helped turn immune checkpoint inhibition from a scientific hypothesis into a clinical reality. For many patients, it has meant years of life that previously had few options at all. But that is only one part of the story. The other part is far less comfortable. Keytruda is not just a breakthrough drug. It is also a striking example of how the contemporary pharmaceutical system works: publicly funded science lays the foundation, private firms take control of the resulting assets, monopoly rights determine pricing, and health systems are then forced to pay extraordinary sums to access medicines they helped make possible in the first place. This is what makes Keytruda so politically important. It is not merely a story about scientific success. It is a story about ownership, public subsidy, corporate strategy, and the growing gap between biomedical progress and equitable access. In that sense, Keytruda is not an exception. It is one of the clearest illustrations of the current system’s structural logic. The science was public before the profits were private The foundations of Keytruda were laid long before Merck turned it into a blockbuster. The crucial scientific breakthrough came with the discovery of PD-1 by Tasuku Honjo and colleagues at Kyoto University in the early 1990s. Over time , this work revealed that PD-1 was part of the immune checkpoint machinery that restrains T-cell activity. That insight fundamentally changed cancer immunology. It suggested that instead of attacking tumors directly, medicine could work by releasing the brakes on the immune system. Read more: Against the normalization of limited access to CAR-T cell therapies This was not the product of isolated corporate brilliance. It resulted from decades of publicly funded research. Government support in Japan sustained Honjo’s work. In the United States , public funding helped establish the wider domain of immune checkpoint research. University laboratories, academic medical centers, and publicly funded research infrastructures made the field possible long before pharmaceutical firms recognized its full commercial value. That matters because the myth of drug innovation frequently begins too late in the story. It starts at the clinical trial, the patent filing, or the approval announcement, rather than at where innovation usually begins: in publicly supported science, collective knowledge production, and institutions built for the public good. Keytruda emerged from that ecosystem. Without it, there would have been nothing for the industry to commercialize. The market did not automatically recognize Keytruda’s value Another revealing aspect of the Keytruda story is that the drug was nearly lost not because the science failed, but because corporate priorities shifted. The antibody that became pembrolizumab originated at Organon, initially in a program not even designed for oncology. Through mergers and acquisitions, it passed to Schering-Plough and then to Merck. During these periods, the program was deprioritized, sidelined, and reportedly nearly discarded altogether. This should give pause to anyone who assumes that private ownership naturally distributes resources to the most socially valuable innovations. Under a system driven by portfolio logic, mergers and stockholder expectations, even a future life-saving therapy can be neglected if it doesn’t fit immediate strategic calculations. Big Pharma greed keeps lifesaving drugs out of reach for millions in the Global South. Source: ITPC/Facebook Pembrolizumab survived not because the market perfectly understood its promise, but because a handful of committed scientists persisted and external developments forced management to reconsider. Once competing checkpoint therapies began to show promise, Merck moved rapidly. What had been treated as marginal suddenly became central. This is often celebrated as corporate agility. But it can just as easily be read as evidence of structural irrationality. A therapy that would go on to become the world’s top-selling drug was almost abandoned because the system is not designed to maximize public health. It is designed to manage financial risk and competitive advantage. From breakthrough to blockbuster Once Merck committed to pembrolizumab, it did so aggressively. The company rapidly expanded the clinical program , scaled up trials , employed biomarker strategies with considerable success, and leveraged regulatory mechanisms to accelerate approval. Scientifically and operationally, this phase proved impressive. It helped bring a major therapeutic advance to patients faster than would otherwise have been possible. That achievement should not be dismissed. It shows that large-scale clinical development, regulatory coordination, and manufacturing capacity remain essential parts of turning promising science into real treatments. The question is not whether these capacities are needed. The question is who controls them, whose interests they serve, and who reaps the rewards. Because once Keytruda succeeded, the rewards were immense. Read more: Patents, profits and squabbles for share in the pie – Moderna’s pandemic story By 2024, it had become the world’s top-selling medicine, generating nearly 29.5 billion USD in annual sales. That figure is astonishing not only because of its scale, but because it reveals how enormous the extractive potential of pharmaceutical monopolies can be when attached to a clinically transformative product. And yet, even this commercial success was built on a landscape formed by public input . The scientific foundations were public. Clinical trial ecosystems depended heavily on academic hospitals and publicly subsidized research environments. Regulatory acceleration came through public institutions. The risks were socialized at crucial stages, but the financial gains were overwhelmingly privatized. A medicine can be revolutionary and still be exclusionary The great paradox of Keytruda is that a drug capable of redefining cancer care can simultaneously remain not accessible to many of the people who need it. In the United States, treatment costs have exceeded 150,000 USD per patient per year. In Europe , health systems have had to negotiate rebates , confidential agreements , and special reimbursement arrangements to contain budgetary impact. Even wealthy countries struggle to absorb the costs of widespread access. For lower-income countries, the situation is far worse. There, access is often minimal, delayed, or effectively nonexistent. This is not a side issue. It is central to how we should evaluate medical innovation. Read more: Not Omicron but greed of capital threatens the world A therapy cannot be judged only by its efficacy in clinical trials or its scientific sophistication. We must also judge it by whether patients can actually receive it. A drug that exists in principle but remains unreachable in practice is not a complete public health success. Keytruda’s inclusion on the WHO Essential Medicines List should have been a powerful recognition of its importance . But that recognition also exposed a deeper contradiction. What does it mean for a medicine to be considered essential if it remains priced beyond the reach of most of the world? At that point, the designation risks becoming symbolic. A medicine can be clinically essential and commercially exclusionary at the same time. Under the present model, that contradiction is not accidental. It is built into the system. The real question is not whether industry matters, but on what terms Defenders of the status quo often respond with a familiar argument: without patents, high prices, and private investment, drugs like Keytruda would never have reached patients. The claim that large-scale development requires resources, coordination, and risk-bearing has some truth. But that does not settle the matter. It merely restates the rules of the current system as if they were laws of nature. They are not. Read more: When Brazilian health workers discovered Soviet healthcare The issue is not whether clinical development and manufacturing require serious investment. Of course they do. The issue is whether public institutions must always play a subordinate role: finance early discovery, de-risk innovation, build research infrastructure, and then step aside once commercialization begins. Why should taxpayers fund the science, support the research ecosystem, and absorb part of the development risk, only to lose all control over pricing, licensing, and access at the decisive moment? Why should a medicine built on public knowledge become a private asset governed by monopoly logic? And why should governments then pay again, at inflated prices, to buy back access for their own populations? These are not radical questions. They are the basic questions that any serious public-interest pharmaceutical policy must confront. Public Pharma is not a fantasy but a necessary direction This is where the idea of Public Pharma becomes more than a slogan. It becomes a practical and moral challenge to the current order . A Public Pharma approach would begin from a simple premise: if public institutions are central to the creation of breakthrough medicines, they should not relinquish stewardship when those medicines become commercially valuable. Public actors should have the capacity not only to fund discovery, but also to shape development, retain ownership stakes, set access conditions, and, where appropriate, support manufacturing and distribution. That would not mean excluding scientific collaboration or denying the complexity of drug development. It would mean changing the terms of engagement. Under such a model, the benefits of a drug like Keytruda could be organized differently. Public investment could come with enforceable conditions on affordability and licensing. Intellectual property could be structured to prevent extreme monopoly control over entire therapeutic pathways. Revenues could be reinvested into further research rather than extracted as shareholder value. Health systems could negotiate from a position of public stewardship rather than defensive purchasing. Most importantly, access would no longer be treated as an afterthought. A breakthrough for whom? Keytruda demonstrates what biomedical science can achieve at its best. It shows that diseases once regarded as almost uniformly fatal can be confronted in entirely new ways. That should be acknowledged without hesitation. But Keytruda also shows the limits of celebrating innovation while ignoring political economy. A medicine can be scientifically brilliant and socially unjust at the same time. It can save lives while still comprising a system that rations access through price. It can stand as proof of human inventiveness while also revealing how poorly that ingenuity is governed. That is why Keytruda should be remembered not only as a triumph of immuno-oncology. It should also be understood as a case study in the contradictions of pharmaceutical capitalism. The lesson is not that we need less innovation. The lesson is that we need a different system for governing it. The real measure of a medical breakthrough is not only whether it can be invented, patented, and sold at scale. It is whether we can make it available, sustainably and fairly, to all who need it. On that question, Keytruda remains not only a success story but an unfinished indictment. David Franco is a scientist and public health activist based in Belgium. In the People’s Health Movement, he focuses on the Public Pharma for Europe (PPfE) initiative. David holds a PhD in Pharmaceutical Sciences from the Free University of Brussels.
